rows.description: A wise approach is to prioritise safety, keep routines, share only what feels right and choose a trained therapist. Recovery is not forgetting; it is the past losing its grip.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17

rows.subtype: Sadness after a loss in children [Actor]
rows.description: A child grieving a grandparent may cry, play happily, then ask the same question again. Grief moves in waves and children need honest simple words and routine; it is normal, not a fault.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager who lost someone feels sadness, anger and guilt, with moments of laughter that bring shame. Grief tends to be tied to the loss and eases with support, while it needs attention if sadness spreads to everything and self-worth collapses.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: amusement, sadness, grief, anger

rows.description: A supportive person notices if months later the person cannot function, feels worthless or hopeless beyond the loss, or speaks of not wanting to live. They encourage professional help; grief and depression can occur together.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A community that gathers for rites and shared meals gives structure to loss. Observers who let people cry, speak of the person and do not hurry them support grief; those who say be strong may isolate the mourner.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: sadness, grief, loneliness

rows.description: A teenager compares their body to filtered images, avoids mirrors or gatherings and links worth to appearance. Feeling badly about body is common; when thoughts take over the day, it is time to seek help.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22

rows.description: A parent or friend notices skipped meals, secrecy around food or constant talk about shape. Expressing care and concern, without commenting on the body or forcing food, and encouraging medical support is wiser.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22

rows.description: A young adult may use rigid rules or secret behaviour with food to cope with stress, shame or a need for control. It brings temporary relief and real harm, and a doctor or specialist is the right place to start.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17

rows.description: A person teased or praised for their body learns that appearance is their value, and can feel watched at every meal. Kindness, and talk about health rather than looks, changes the climate.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17

rows.subtype: Building a kinder relationship with the body [Response]
rows.description: A wise approach values what the body can do, limits harsh social media, eats regular meals and speaks kindly of self. When the struggle is serious, a qualified professional is essential.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17
